item.title: Directional and Quasi-Omnidirectional Indoor Channel Measurements at Upper 6 GHz
item.description: arXiv:2610.14890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical directional and quasi-omnidirectional antenna pairs are compared at 6.425--7.125 GHz over 32 position-matched indoor links per configuration: 23 line-of-sight (LOS) and nine non-LOS (NLOS) links in an open hall and an L-shaped corridor. Peak-gain normalization retains antenna-pattern weighting in the measured path loss, shadow-fading residuals, RMS delay spread (DS), and PDP-equivalent $K$ factor. Hall LOS close-in exponents are nearly identical at 2.10/2.11 for directional\slash quasi-omnidirectional pairs, yet median DS values differ markedly at 1.78/36.52 ns. Directional DS is lower at all LOS positions, with smaller fitted shadow-fading residuals and higher $K$ factors. Representative PDPs associate these differences with reduced off-axis delayed energy. In corridor NLOS, the directional floating-intercept slope is negative, consistent with distance-dependent antenna-pattern weighting under the fixed pointing rule, whereas the quasi-omnidirectional slope is positive and DS ordering varies by position. These results quantify practical antenna-filtered channels without angular-scan synthesis, with unequal weak-path sensitivity contributing to the observed differences.
item.dc:creator: Chengsong Fu, Hongbo Zhao, Jianer Zhou, Xiongbin Yu, Weichao Li, Chen Zhuang, Meng Li, Wenquan Feng, Xiaofeng Tao

item.title: Localized Joule heating and carbonization process optimization of 3D printed polymer structures for lab-on-CMOS applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.15238v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Use of carbon electrodes integrated with CMOS technology has great promise for lab-on-chip, biomedical, environmental, and industrial applications. One method of developing carbon electrodes is to 3D print polymer nanostructures on a CMOS chip, and use a thermal annealing process to pyrolyze them into carbon at high temperature, approximately 950 {\deg}C. Such high temperature is detrimental to the CMOS sensor circuits, causing severe degradation. We present a novel solution of localized Joule heating of these polymer nanostructures to achieve complete carbonization of the electrodes. Both analytical and COMSOL simulations guided the experiments to characterize the carbonization process conditions. Partial carbonization was achieved at 500-600 {\deg}C of global temperature, and complete carbonization was achieved by localized Joule heating. Pyrolized nanostructures monolithic samples on a silica wafer were fabricated using standard material processing, such as 2-Photon Polymerization. Pyrolysis was achieved by Rapid Thermal Processing (RTP). Observations using optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and Raman spectroscopy demonstrated the feasibility of polymer carbonization within a CMOS compatible temperature window.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Aminul Haque, Andalib Nizam, Nickolay Lavrik, Nicole Mcfarlane

item.title: Toward Partitioned Reference Readout for Four-Level IGZO Memory: Device Statistics, Confusion Matrices, and INT4 Error Propagation
item.description: arXiv:2610.16255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Four-level indium-gallium-zinc oxide (IGZO) 2T0C memory needs reliable state formation, sensing references, and a path from cell errors to digital weights. We analyze 107 measured DC transfer curves from 37 isolated IGZO transistors (W/L = 3/0.5 micrometers). Four gate-bias operating points inferred from the first sweep are evaluated on later sweeps of 35 devices. Device-resolved operating points reduce second-sweep across-device current standard deviation by 49.4-52.4%, yet retaining initial thresholds increases misclassified points from 37/140 to 55/140. Leave-one-device-out reference estimation gives 0/140 on the second sweep; freezing second-sweep thresholds yields 6/140 on the third. Sampling eight reference transistors on the third sweep gives a mean held-out error fraction of 0.15% over 2,000 selections, versus 4.33% with frozen thresholds on matched held-out devices. We present conditional confusion matrices, a counterfactual common-gain sensitivity, and an INT4 error-propagation proxy. A simultaneous four-state bank with eight reference cells per state requires at least 32 physical reference cells, 12.5% of a proposed 256-cell data bank before peripheral overhead. A charge-conservation model and a partitioned hierarchical error model specify the pulse, retention, and array measurements needed to test transfer from DC device statistics to pulsed 2T0C operation.
item.dc:creator: Huiyun Li

item.title: Neuromorphic Decoding and Dynamical Image Reconstruction from Populations of Spiking Retinal Ganglion Cells
item.description: arXiv:2610.17154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decoding visual stimuli from the spiking activity of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) informs both our understanding of the retinal code and the design of visual prostheses. Natural vision is dynamic, yet state-of-the-art decoders mostly reconstruct single frames with artificial neural networks that process dense, continuous-valued signals rather than the retina's sparse, asynchronous spikes. We asked whether dynamic scenes can be reconstructed and tracked entirely within the spike domain, and at what computational cost. We built an end-to-end spiking neural network (SNN) whose neurons integrate the recorded RGC spikes over time. Populations of up to 1836 RGCs were recorded ex vivo from mouse retina on high-density microelectrode arrays while flashed images, moving bars, drifting gratings and randomly moving handwritten digits were presented. For moving digits, one shared spiking encoder fed two readouts, one reconstructing the image and one decoding the digit's position. Compute energy was estimated from counted synaptic operations. The SNN decoded what and where at once. It reconstructed the stimuli with a structural similarity (SSIM) of up to 0.93, refining the reconstruction as spikes accumulated, and tracked a randomly moving target with a mean error of 1.33 pixels on a $32\times32$ grid. Its fidelity nearly matched that of the best of 17 larger spiking and artificial decoders (5.9 million to 1.7 billion parameters, versus 5.4 million), and at a mean firing rate of 14.2% it needed an estimated $\sim$70-fold less compute energy than a dense artificial network of the same architecture. Dynamic visual scenes can thus be decoded from retinal population activity in the spike domain, with a compact network and at a compute cost compatible with implantable and wearable neural interfaces, supporting spike-native decoders for visual prostheses.
item.dc:creator: Ning Zhang, Arto Nurmikko

item.title: PRIM: Energy- and Endurance-Aware Compiler Optimization for Digital Compute in Non-volatile Memory
item.description: arXiv:2610.17167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compute-in-Memory (CiM) is an alternative computing paradigm that circumvents the memory bandwidth bottleneck. Variants utilizing non-volatile memory cells (NVCiM) to perform Boolean operations directly within memory arrays offer significant density and energy-efficiency advantages. Fully realizing this potential, however, requires NVCiM-specific compiler optimizations. In conventional digital NVCiM systems, an output cell must be written -- or preset -- to an operation-specific value before any Boolean operation can occur. Preset-induced extra writes can degrade energy efficiency and cell endurance, often to the point of negating CiM's efficiency gains. In this paper, we introduce PRIM (Preset Reduction In Memory), a compiler optimization framework tailored for digital NVCiM that effectively minimizes preset overhead without compromising computational accuracy or architectural complexity. Unlike existing optimization approaches, PRIM is not restricted to specific types of Boolean operations. Experimental results show that PRIM can reduce execution time and energy consumption by up to 50/% and 44/%, respectively, while boosting cell endurance by up to 50/%.
item.dc:creator: Patrick Miller, Ulya R. Karpuzcu

item.title: Two-State Dynamical Synapses as a Physical Substrate for Equilibrium Propagation
item.description: arXiv:2610.18058v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Equilibrium Propagation (EqProp) updates each synapse by comparing a local term at the free and nudged equilibria. Because these two values occur at different times, a physical implementation requires temporary local memory. We show that this memory can emerge from a two-timescale synaptic model in which neural and volatile synaptic dynamics are jointly derived from a single energy function. A volatile state $w$ relaxes toward the product of the pre- and postsynaptic activities, while a non-volatile state $M$ stores the learned parameter. At equilibrium, $w$ equals the local term entering the EqProp update. Using its net change between phases implements phase-based EqProp, while transferring its successive changes during nudging yields continual EqProp, in which the temporal comparison is carried by the synaptic dynamics themselves. On MNIST with a single-hidden-layer network, the phase-based model reaches $2.01 \pm 0.09\%$ test error versus $2.00 \pm 0.13\%$ for standard EqProp, and the continual model reaches $2.24 \pm 0.11\%$ versus $2.28 \pm 0.16\%$ for continual EqProp. The framework further specifies the dynamical requirements that a volatile--non-volatile synaptic device must satisfy to implement this learning mechanism.
item.dc:creator: Dongshu Liu, Julie Grollier

item.title: PotentialEP: Backprop-Free Training of CIFAR-Scale Generative Models via Equilibrium Propagation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14409v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generating an image with a diffusion or flow-matching model typically involves integrating a velocity field for hundreds of sequential steps. That computation suits a GPU poorly and an analog neuromorphic substrate well, where one fast, low-power physical relaxation could replace the whole sequence. Two things are needed: a generative algorithm whose computation is a relaxation, and a way to train it without backpropagation, whose global gradient transport is hard to realise in analog. Energy Matching supplies the first, sampling by gradient-descent relaxation on a time-independent potential - but obtaining the gradient that descent follows is itself a backward pass, once per integration step. We prove that a predictive coding network with a single linear injection term added to its energy relaxes to a state whose visible layer carries that gradient inherently, with an error that vanishes for small injection strengths. An Energy Matching model trained by backpropagation can therefore be loaded into this network unchanged and sampled by relaxation alone, matching the original model's FID to within 0.04 at CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 scale. The network can also be trained without backpropagation: Equilibrium Propagation reproduces backpropagation's parameter updates to a cosine similarity of 0.9998, and training end to end with those updates reaches an FID of 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 against 3.54 for backpropagation. To our knowledge this is the first CIFAR-10 generative model trained with Equilibrium Propagation, and the first at competitive quality by any backpropagation-free rule. This quality does not require group normalisation or attention: an architecture of only convolutions and pointwise nonlinearities, both native to an analog crossbar, reaches an FID of 3.51 when trained by backpropagation.
item.dc:creator: Alex Gower

item.title: UAV-Mounted Hybrid RIS-Assisted ISAC-RSMA: Performance Analysis with Imperfect CSI and SIC
item.description: arXiv:2610.15072v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems, strict sensing requirements can substantially constrain the transmit power available for communication. A hybrid reconfigurable intelligent surface (HRIS) with passive reflection and active amplification capabilities mounted on an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) can enhance coverage and strengthen communication links in such power-limited regimes. Meanwhile, rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) provides an effective transmission strategy for managing inter-user interference, particularly in dense multiuser wireless scenarios. Motivated by this, we analyze the performance of a UAV-mounted HRIS-assisted monostatic ISAC system employing RSMA scheme. We consider the imperfections in the channel state information and successive interference cancellation in the RSMA, which are inevitable in practical system implementations. We then derive highly accurate expressions for outage probability, ergodic rate, and throughput to evaluate communication performance over Nakagami-$m$ fading channels. These expressions reveal key insights into the diversity order and coding gain of the system in the high signal-to-noise ratio regime. To characterize the sensing performance, we derive expressions for the probability of detection, the probability of false alarm, and the Cram\'er-Rao lower bound. Numerical results validate the theoretical findings and highlight the performance gains of the proposed system over conventional multiple-access schemes and RIS-based systems.
item.dc:creator: Chandan Kumar Singh, Arthur Sousa de Sena, Smriti Uniyal, Deepak Kumar, Prabhat K. Upadhyay, Matti Latva-aho

item.title: TurnCost: Turns, Not Observations: Cache-Aware Loop Engineering for Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.15093v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI coding agents operate in iterative loops: they modify code, run tools, inspect the results, and decide what to do next. We call the design of this process loop engineering, which includes context management, model selection, compaction, and termination. Existing efficiency work mainly compresses tool observations or routes selected turns to cheaper models, but the practical opportunity for these optimizations remains unclear. We analyze 600 publicly released coding-agent trajectories spanning two agent scaffolds and two language models. Median observations contain only 118-286 tokens, while the large build logs commonly used to motivate compression occur near the ninety-ninth percentile. Moreover, 98.6% of input tokens are served from a prefix cache, so flat input pricing overestimates loop cost by roughly 7x on average under near-ideal caching. We derive and empirically validate a closed-form break-even condition for model delegation. Delegation increases cost in half of the evaluated settings, near the predicted boundary. More broadly, turn count explains 84% of the variance in log trajectory cost, compared with 4% for mean observation size; the most expensive trajectories have the most turns despite having the smallest observations. These associations suggest that observation-focused methods target a secondary cost factor, and identify unnecessary turns as the larger and largely unexamined opportunity, though we do not establish that turns can be removed while holding task success fixed. We release TurnCost, a tool for re-scoring trajectory corpora under alternative caching, pricing, compression, and routing policies.
item.dc:creator: Pramod Kumar, Raj Kumar Pandey

item.title: Generative Quantum Machine Learning Methods for Cancer Detection using Augmented Datasets
item.description: arXiv:2610.15110v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cancer detection using AI methods and image databases faces several challenges, including limited and imbalanced image datasets, long algorithm training times, and high-complexity feature generation. In particular, many cancer image datasets contain very few malignant examples compared to benign ones, limiting the amount of minority-class data available for training. Although classical AI and especially deep learning methods have had some success in providing cancer diagnostics, Quantum Machine Learning (QML) methods may offer advantages through high-dimensional feature representations, generative data augmentation, and the exploitation of feature correlations through quantum properties such as entanglement. In this paper, we propose using a generative QML method on the compressed breast ultrasound image dataset (BUSI) to generate synthetic images and hence augmented datasets for classifier training. In particular, we train a convolutional neural network with real, synthetic, and a combination of real and synthetic images. We test the algorithm on real images and provide comparative results for all three training cases. Our results show that the classifier trained entirely on synthetic images achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.802 (80.2%), compared with 0.760 (76.0%) for the real-data baseline.
item.dc:creator: Sophia Knutson, Nandika Goyal, Gennaro De Luca, Glen Uehara, Tanay Kamlesh Patel, Andreas Spanias

item.title: Stateless Stochastic Computing for Generative AI on Superconducting Logic: A Model-Hardware Co-Design
item.description: arXiv:2610.15392v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Thermodynamic computing lets stochastic physical dynamics carry out a computation and reads out the result as a time average. Recently, thermodynamic computing has been demonstrated on several hardware platforms, including digital CMOS circuits based on stochastic computing. Superconducting single-flux-quantum (SFQ) logic offers very high clock rates and very low switching energy, but it heavily penalizes state, memory, fan-out, and feedback, i.e., exactly the per-neuron accumulators on which such designs rely. We therefore realize thermodynamic computing in SFQ logic through a co-design of a generative model and its circuit in which the datapath holds no state at all. The model is a class-conditional flow-matching image generator, which transforms Gaussian noise into an image of the requested class along a short, deterministic path of four Euler steps; in hardware, these steps are unrolled into a feed-forward pipeline of stochastic bitstream operators, whose output is read out as a time average, as in thermodynamic computing, without any relaxation phase. Each layer of the model is a butterfly-factorized linear map built exclusively from multiplexers that operate on split-unipolar bitstreams. The ReLU activation, which in stochastic computing requires a per-neuron up/down counter (accounting for 60-70% of the JJs in a counter-based design), is replaced by a stateless AND-NOT gate whose one-clock input skew is provided at no cost by SFQ gate-level pipelining. The models are trained directly on the stream representation of the hardware, with a regularizer that bounds the stream gains. Synthesis with an SFQ design flow shows that stochastic streams tolerate relaxed path balancing, which reduces the Josephson-junction (JJ) count of a hard-wired stage by 40-47%.
item.dc:creator: Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram

item.title: Tracing Money Flows in the Multi-Token Cryptocurrency Network
item.description: arXiv:2610.16981v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tracing money flows in cryptocurrency transaction networks is challenging because funds can move across accounts, transactions, and token layers. We propose a transaction-aware graph in which nodes represent account--asset states within transactions, while edges encode observed transfers, inferred asset transformations, and temporal inter-transaction sequences. Applied to Aave borrow--repay flows, we compare graph construction and edge-pruning strategies and extract shortest paths using a heuristic weighting. Our results reveal a trade-off between reachability and interpretability and uncover frequent token sequences underlying how borrowed assets are transformed before repayment. This work lays a foundation for general, interpretable multi-token flow tracing.
item.dc:creator: Natkamon Tovanich, C\'{e}lestin Coquid\'{e}

item.title: Architecting Instruction Execution for Scalable Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
item.description: arXiv:2610.17058v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) requires orchestrating millions of operations continuously across a tightly coupled classical-quantum control stack. A critical challenge in this orchestration is determining the optimal hardware-software boundary, i.e., the Quantum Instruction Set Architecture (QISA). We focus on cryogenic, fixed-connectivity qubit platforms, such as superconducting and topological Majorana qubits. For these, existing QISA choices either operate at too low a level, violating cryogenic thermal budgets at scale, or at too high a level, imposing unrealizable complexity on the control engine. To reason about these tradeoffs, we introduce the ARIES instruction set hierarchy, which categorizes QISAs into distinct abstraction levels. To systematically evaluate these levels, we develop an end-to-end evaluation toolflow featuring a cycle-accurate classical driver and hardware engine simulator. Using eight quantum applications across superconducting and topological qubit platforms, we measure instruction bandwidth, transceiver power dissipation, and measurement processing overheads. We demonstrate that while physical-level abstractions exceed the thermal limits of dilution refrigerators by orders of magnitude, canonical-level abstractions significantly underestimate hardware routing congestion and execution runtimes. Our Level 4 QISA (local logical operations) offers an optimal architectural balance. As quantum hardware platforms scale toward FTQC in the coming years, our findings provide concrete architectural guidance for the design of their classical control stacks and instruction interfaces.
item.dc:creator: Dmitry Filippov, Justin Hogaboam, Mathias Soeken, Raghu Gatta, Prakash Murali, Matthias Troyer

item.title: PADO-Pauli: A GPU-Accelerated Implementation of Pauli Propagation
item.description: arXiv:2610.17755v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Variational quantum algorithms utilize parameterized circuits many times during training, at new parameter values, over batches of data, and with gradients. Pauli propagation approximates the expectation values of such circuits classically by evolving the observable in the Heisenberg picture as a truncated sum of Pauli strings. We present PADO-Pauli, a GPU engine for Pauli propagation that compiles a circuit and its observables once into sparse matrices in which each rotation angle contributes only a cosine and a sine factor, so every later evaluation reuses the compiled program. It evaluates batches of parameters and data inputs embedded as rotation angles. By default its gradients come from a vector-Jacobian product registered with PyTorch's automatic differentiation, so they flow through the angles to any classical layer that produces them. PADO-Pauli also provides truncation by Pauli weight and coefficient size, and noise channels. Zero-filtering removes terms that do not contribute to an expectation value in the all-zero reference state and makes the batched forward pass about 1.5 times faster. Compared to cuPauliProp on an NVIDIA A100, PADO-Pauli evaluates up to 10 times faster on 4 to 12 qubits and uses up to 3.1 times less memory on 16 qubits. We check its accuracy against exact statevector simulation up to 28 qubits. These features make PADO-Pauli a practical toolkit for training variational quantum algorithms, including quantum machine learning models.
item.dc:creator: Hyunwoo Kim, Youngseok Lee

item.title: Lifting: Quantum State Discrimination Framework for Mid-Circuit Measurements
item.description: arXiv:2610.18482v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum computing promises new capabilities beyond classical computation. Mid-circuit measurements (MCMs) enable error correction and outcome-dependent control, but their reliability is limited by noise on superconducting hardware. These operations depend on accurate quantum state discrimination (QSD), which assigns measured signals to state labels. Neural network-based (NN-based) QSD improves this assignment, yet its error remains bounded below by the Bayes risk of the available readout distributions. A complementary challenge is state deterioration as successive measurements accumulate and circuit execution advances, making static calibration less representative of the workload. We present Lifting, a QSD framework that addresses both challenges through repetition encoding, neural decoding, and in situ calibration. Encoding supplies joint in-phase and quadrature (I-Q) readout signals from the target and auxiliary qubits, while contextual calibration trains the decoder for the conditions encountered during execution. Our theoretical analysis shows that retaining additional channels from a fixed joint distribution cannot increase Bayes risk and establishes sufficient conditions for contraction of an overlap-based upper bound. Experiments across three IBM processors evaluate the framework on repeated stabilizer measurement, parity-check, and teleportation workloads.
item.dc:creator: Chi Zhang, Neel Vora, Yilun Xu, Gang Huang, Fan Chen, Lei Jiang

item.title: HILO: Enabling Low-power, Dual-Band Communication using Tunnel Diode Oscillators
item.description: arXiv:2610.18641v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wireless communication remains the most power-consuming operation in embedded systems. Low-power transmitters such as backscatter achieve microwatt-scale operation but produce weak signals susceptible to in-band interference and frequency-selective fading, particularly in non-line-of-sight settings. Multi-band transmission can mitigate these effects through spectral-domain redundancy rather than temporal-domain redundancy, improving reliability without sacrificing bitrate or latency. However, conventional multi-band radio transceivers require duplicated RF chains or power-hungry synthesizers. We introduce HILO, a tunnel diode-based frontend that enables dual-band operation from a single circuit. HILO inverts the conventional paradigm: rather than suppressing the harmonics inherent to tunnel diode nonlinearity, it harnesses them. An external device injection-locks the oscillator to a fundamental frequency, simultaneously stabilizing a higher harmonic and yielding two injection-locked carriers without a second oscillator or frequency multiplier. In transmit mode, HILO exploits self-oscillating mixing to modulate both carriers simultaneously; in receive mode, it uses autodyne downconversion at both frequencies. By turning an inherent nonlinearity into a feature, HILO achieves dual-band links while consuming under 210 $\mu$W.
item.dc:creator: Dhairya Shah, Rajashekar Reddy Chinthalapani, Pramuka Sooriya Patabandige, Ambuj Varshney

item.title: Bio-Inspired Electrotactile Feedback: A Framework and Impacts of Multimodal Cues
item.description: arXiv:2610.18746v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Electrotactile stimulation, as a haptic feedback method, often struggles to evoke high-quality natural sensations. Consequently, despite its practical advantages, it is generally less preferred in human-machine systems than mechanical approaches. In this paper, we propose a bio-inspired stimulation framework that generates signals modelled on afferent neural activity derived from a touch model. By producing more biologically plausible spiking patterns, the proposed approach aims to enhance the realism of perceived tactile sensations. To evaluate these stimulation patterns in a realistic task context and to quantify the influence of visual and movement cues, we conducted a series of subjective experiments under three conditions. The results indicate that bio-inspired modulation was effective: in particular, bio-inspired co-modulation of amplitude and frequency achieved a favourable pressure-irritation trade-off, increasing the probability of perceiving pressure while maintaining low irritation (pressure: 0.78; irritation: 0.24) relative to the other patterns. Visual cues and hand movement further improved feedback quality by significantly increasing the probability of reporting pressure (p$<$0.001) without a corresponding increase in irritation, and by increasing mean naturalness ratings. Overall, these findings demonstrate the potential of bio-inspired electrotactile patterns to improve haptic feedback quality, and highlight the importance of evaluating such methods under realistic, multimodal interaction scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Melika Emami, Amirhossein Bayat, Rahim Tafazolli, Atta Quddus

item.title: Source Distance and Source Strength Estimation in Turbulent Flow: Exploiting Molecule Degradation Diversity
item.description: arXiv:2604.15032v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Locating an odor source and estimating its strength are central problems in nature and engineering. For example, an insect may decide whether a food source is worth traveling to based on its distance and how many molecules it emits. Similarly, a drone or sensor network may need to locate a pipe leak and quantify how much chemical is released. Such tasks are highly challenging due to complex turbulent propagation dynamics. While source distance and strength estimation have been extensively investigated for sources releasing a single molecule type, in both turbulent and non-turbulent flow, many odor sources release multiple molecule types. We investigate whether considering multiple molecule types can aid source distance and strength estimation in challenging turbulent flow. We exploit that different molecule types in a mixture degrade at different rates in the atmosphere. Consequently, the relative abundance of the molecule types observed at a receiver provides information about the source distance that a single molecule type does not. Since this relative abundance is independent of the source strength, it resolves the distance-strength ambiguity inherent in the observed signal intensity and thus also improves strength estimation. Building on this, we propose heuristic low-complexity and learning-based schemes that combine the relative abundance of different molecule types with established features such as mean concentration and whiff duration. All schemes are validated via simulations of turbulent molecule propagation. The low-complexity schemes can achieve estimation quality competitive with learning-based schemes that rely only on a single molecule type, while the proposed learning-based schemes outperform their single-type counterparts. Molecule mixtures can therefore support goal-oriented tasks such as source distance and strength estimation even in challenging turbulent flow.
item.dc:creator: Bastian Heinlein, Timo Jakumeit, Robert Schober, Maximilian Sch\"afer, Vahid Jamali

item.title: GPU-Accelerated Quantum Annealing-Inspired UAV Path Planning for Smart Agriculture
item.description: arXiv:2608.25376v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: With the rapid advancement of smart agriculture, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have become indispensable for efficient coverage and path planning in grid-mapped agricultural fields. However, optimizing UAV flight paths in large-scale environments remains a complex Nondeterministic Polynomial-time (NP)-hard problem. Traditional path planning methods are often constrained by local optima, limited scalability, and slow convergence, which significantly restrict their effectiveness in solving large-scale problems. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel optimization framework utilizing a Graphics Processing Unit (GPU)-parallelized Ising solver. Our method mimics the operational principles of quantum annealing on GPU hardware, enabling rapid search for the minimum-energy state of Ising models. Unlike physical quantum devices, which are often constrained by the number of qubits, our approach leverages the Fixstars Amplify (FA) platform to perform parallel annealing on highly parallelized GPUs. This enables the simultaneous evaluation of thousands of potential path candidates and vast state transitions. By leveraging large-scale parallel processing, this framework's core strength lies in minimizing computation time even as the problem scale increases. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed method consistently identifies superior flight paths while maintaining stable computational performance compared with the genetic algorithm and simulated annealing method.
item.dc:creator: Maho Hirahara, Aohan Li

item.title: FractalNet-Based Heterogeneous Federated Learning for Orbital Edge Intelligence in Satellite Mega-Constellations: A Wildfire Case Study
item.description: arXiv:2609.00875v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Satellite mega-constellations are emerging as large-scale sensing, communication, and computation fabrics, yet their learning architectures remain largely inherited from terrestrial federated learning and ground-centric mission operations--- ill-suited to satellites that differ by orders of magnitude in Size, Weight, Power, and Cost (SWAP-C), radiation tolerance, link availability, and propagation delay. We propose a heterogeneous federated learning method based on the FractalNet architecture for orbital edge intelligence. We formalize contact-window-constrained, depth-heterogeneous federated optimization and introduce a distributed path scheduler that assigns model depth as a function of SWAP-C constraints, predicted inter-satellite contacts, and training statistics. To reduce message overhead and energy consumption, each tier pools updates periodically rather than at every contact opportunity, and a three-tier agentic control plane governs in-space scheduling, anomaly escalation, and policy-governed autonomy. As a case study, we apply the framework to wildfire detection, where each orbital shell naturally learns a different semantic level of situational awareness: pixel-scale thermal anomalies at low Earth orbit (LEO), regional fire-front dynamics at medium Earth orbit (MEO), and larger-scale risk propagation at geostationary or high Earth orbit (GEO/HEO). Experiments on simulated mega-constellations validate the approach across convergence, communication efficiency, energy adaptation, scheduled-pooling savings, robustness, and latency.
item.dc:creator: Sai Puppala, Bhabani P. Sinha, Koushik Sinha

item.title: A Backend-Agnostic MWIS Kernel for Stochastic Unit Commitment with Neutral-Atom Hardware Validation
item.description: arXiv:2609.01248v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum hardware is beginning to address structured combinatorial optimisation, but two steps still block practical use: mapping real operational models onto hardware-compatible instances, and converting noisy hardware output back into feasible decisions. Here we introduce a backend-agnostic computational interface that compiles the discrete decision layer of stochastic unit commitment into a move-based maximum-weight independent set (MWIS) problem, while retaining continuous dispatch and feasibility recovery in the classical computational layer. We validate the approach in a green hydrogen scheduling setting and deploy it on the QuEra Aquila neutral-atom quantum processor. This is the first end-to-end industrial scheduling workflow that connects real operational decisions to programmable neutral-atom hardware through a solver-agnostic MWIS representation. Across a 15-day hardware campaign on 50-node instances, hardware-generated solutions after classical refinement match or exceed the dispatch margins obtained from exact MWIS on every day. When scaling to 144 nodes, encoding quality remains stable, while the probability that the full atom array survives, rather than graph embedding, emerges as the dominant bottleneck to further scaling. Together, these results establish a hardware-compatible computational pathway toward larger problem scales, and lay the groundwork for exploring regimes in which exact classical optimisation may no longer scale efficiently.
item.dc:creator: Jiying Chen, Min Lin, Jingwei Wen, Zhihong Zhang, Chuixiong Wu

item.title: Reinforcement Learning-Based 3D Beam Adaptation for Underwater Wireless Optical Communication with AUVs
item.description: arXiv:2610.06407v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Underwater Wireless Optical Communications (UWOC) provide essential high data rates for Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs), but reliable connectivity is critically affected by transmitter-receiver misalignment. This work addresses the beam pointing problem for a moving AUV subject to unknown ocean currents through a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework. We develop a comprehensive 3D UWOC channel model incorporating depth-dependent attenuation, turbulence, and a discrete-ray method to accurately quantify geometric and misalignment losses. The resulting agent jointly optimizes beam steering and divergence angles, learning a policy that prioritizes continuous link maintenance. Evaluated using real oceanographic data, the framework's performance is assessed via the excess outage metric, which isolates outages occurring exclusively due to pointing errors. Relative to perfect alignment between nodes, the proposed method bounds this metric to 8.5% under ocean current-free tracking conditions and limits it to 16.2% when subjected to current-induced drift. The findings obtained in this work confirms that DRL-enabled beam control is capable of adaptive tracking and mitigating link outages in dynamic underwater environments.
item.dc:creator: Viviana Centritto, Ama Bandara, Sergi Abadal, Evgenii Vinogradov
